newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND-Russian borrowers plan bond rush in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Russian borrowers plan bond rush in 1997.

text.p: Russian borrowers are planning a rush of bond issues in 1997 but no amount of preparation can influence the main determinant of success, interest rates, analysts said.
"The key thing for Russian borrowers is what happens to the interest rate cycle," a trader at a top European bank said.

"Although rates may rise slightly over the next 12 months, the overall trend is for them to remain low. It is this window the Eastern Europeans (and Russians) need to use in order to establish themselves in the market," he said.
Russia raised $1 billion in the bond market in November, its first international debt issue since the 1917 revolution.
As well as further deals from the government, the cities of Moscow and St Petersburg and companies like Gazprom and LukOil, among others, are expected to issue bonds.

"By the end of 1997 there will be at least a dozen Russian Eurobond issues, enough to form a Russian portfolio with some industry and sector diversification," said Robert Devane, head of fixed income at Russian investment bank Troika Dialog.
"The amount raised will be between $12 and $20 billion, with $12 billion a more realistic expectation," he said.
Investor demand for high-yielding bonds has been insatiable this year but higher rates of interest could stop this trend.
Short-term interest rates are at historically low levels and are expected to remain so into 1997.
"One of the reasons we have had such fantastic demand (for emerging market debt) is the very low German and U.S. government rates," said a banker at a U.S. investment bank.

"Low yields mean investors are more prepared to take on credit risk than if Treasury yields were themselves at eight percent, for example. If rates were to go up, then we would see a sharp fall in demand for emerging market bonds," he said.
But as Russia is included in more emerging market indices, dealers said there would be an automatic pool of demand for its assets as investors struggled to meet index-allocation targets.
"Some demand for Russia is because it is flavour of the day but some is driven by the need to include Russian bonds in indices," said Devane at Troika Dialog.

High Russian yields -- its five-year dollar bond trades 345 basis points (b.p.) or 3.45 percentage points over U.S. Treasuries -- could bring investors to favour Russian rather than other Eastern European debt.

The credit perception of many of these countries has improved dramatically in the last year. Although Russia's credit is expected to get better, it will continue to yield relatively more than other countries, dealers said.

"Russia's credit will improve but it is different to the Czech Republic, where spreads have dropped from 150 basis points over Treasury bonds to 20 or 30 b.p. over," said an emerging market debt trader at a European bank.
"We will not see such a drastic move in Russia, and this will boost demand for its bonds because they will yield in the three digits b.p. over Treasuries for some time," he said.
Meanwhile, a number of obstacles need to be cleared before investors can buy the first non-sovereign Russian debt issue.

"Eurobond investors like to have the comfort there will be no withholding tax but this guarantee cannot yet be given for non-sovereign Russian bonds," said a banker involved in preparing one of next year's bonds.
Troika Dialog's Devane said: "Withholding tax is an issue but I suspect it will be figured out pretty soon because a few of the issuers are due to come to the market in February."
Inefficiencies inside Russia mean the process of getting bonds authorised will remain unpredictable and cumbersome.
"Getting authorisation for deals will continue to be a difficult, arduous task, even once the tax issue is resolved," a trader at a European bank said.
"The high-profile companies, that have political clout, will be able to push for authorisation more easily," he said.

The greater range of Russian credits will give investors the chance to pick and choose. "The market will become more conscious about the actual risk they are taking," said a banker covering Russia at a U.S. bank.

"At the moment you have investors going in because there is nothing out there, there is a lack of paper and they want to get part of the action. People will get more credit conscious and look at what exactly they are buying," he said.
There are bound to be some disappointments.
"There are some potential issuers who are now talking about doing Eurobonds who find it will not be as easy as they thought it was," said a Moscow-based banker.

"This applies to large companies and municipalities. Some will try to drive a Eurobond process through the pipeline only to find their accounts are in such a mess it is not practical for them to come to the Euromarket," he said.
